title: “PAUL SAID HE WASN’T TELLING CHRISTIANS TO AVOID EVERY SEXUALLY IMMORAL PERSON IN THE WORLD”
paragraphs: “PAUL SAID HE WASN’T TELLING CHRISTIANS TO AVOID EVERY SEXUALLY IMMORAL PERSON IN THE WORLD”
We may have spent years avoiding the very people Jesus sent us to reach—while becoming strangely comfortable with unrepentant sin inside the church.
There is a sentence in the Bible that can make religious people uncomfortable.
Not because it excuses sin.
Not because it lowers God's standard.
But because it exposes how easily we can apply God's standard to everybody except the people Paul was actually confronting.
Read this slowly.
Paul was dealing with sexual immorality so serious that he refused to soften his words. Yet in the middle of that confrontation, he stopped to make something unmistakably clear:
When he told Christians not to associate with sexually immoral people...
he was not talking about every sexually immoral person in the world.
That changes the conversation.
Because some of us learned Christianity as though holiness meant staying as far away as possible from sinners.
Don't sit with them.
Don't befriend them.
Don't eat with them.
Don't let people see you around them.
Don't enter their world.
Don't get too close.
And somewhere along the way, separation from sin quietly became separation from sinners.
But then you open 1 Corinthians 5.
And Paul says, essentially:
That isn't what I meant.
The original Greek is painfully clear:
Ἔγραψα ὑμῖν ἐν τῇ ἐπιστολῇ μὴ συναναμίγνυσθαι πόρνοις, οὐ πάντως τοῖς πόρνοις τοῦ κόσμου τούτου...
Egrapsa hymin en tē epistolē mē synanamignysthai pornois, ou pantōs tois pornois tou kosmou toutou...
“I wrote to you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people—not at all meaning the sexually immoral people of this world...”
Then Paul says something almost startling in its simplicity.
If that were what he meant...
you would have to leave the world.
Think about that.
You would have to leave the world.
Paul knew Christians would encounter sexually broken people.
Greedy people.
Idolaters.
Swindlers.
People whose lives were nowhere near God's design.
And his solution was not:
“Disappear.”
It wasn't:
“Build walls high enough that sinners can never reach you.”
It wasn't:
“Only associate with people whose lives already look Christian.”
Because if Christians disappear from the lives of sinners...
who is going to tell sinners about Christ?
This is where the passage becomes uncomfortable in another direction.
Because Paul wasn't becoming permissive.
He wasn't saying sexual immorality doesn't matter.
He wasn't saying, “Who are we to judge?” as though holiness were irrelevant.
Actually, the rest of the chapter destroys that interpretation.
Paul's concern was so serious that he demanded church discipline against a professing believer openly persisting in scandalous sexual sin.
The distinction is everything.
Paul writes:
ἐάν τις ἀδελφὸς ὀνομαζόμενος ᾖ πόρνος...
ean tis adelphos onomazomenos ē pornos...
The force of the words is roughly:
“If anyone being called a brother is sexually immoral...”
There it is.
Paul wasn't primarily talking about the unbeliever who never claimed to follow Jesus.
He was talking about someone wearing the name brother while openly persisting in conduct that contradicted the Lord whose name he claimed.
And suddenly Paul's words become sharper.
Because the scandal in Corinth wasn't simply that sexual sin existed in Corinth.
Of course it existed in Corinth.
The scandal was that serious, unrepentant sin had entered the fellowship of believers...
and the church was tolerating it.
Paul's question cuts through two thousand years of religious hypocrisy:
“For what have I to do with judging outsiders?”
Then:
“Are you not to judge those inside?”
And finally:
“God will judge those outside.”
We have sometimes reversed Paul's order.
We rage at outsiders for behaving like outsiders...
while making excuses for insiders behaving as though Christ has no authority over them.
We become furious when unbelievers don't obey a Bible they don't believe...
then remain strangely quiet when someone who publicly claims Jesus refuses His lordship.
Paul turns the spotlight around.
Stop expecting people who have not surrendered to Christ to behave as though they have already been transformed by Christ.
Give them the Gospel.
Love them enough to tell them the truth.
Walk into their darkness carrying light.
Call sin what God calls sin, yes—but don't forget why Jesus came.
He did not come because humanity was already clean.
He came because we weren't.
Maybe you're reading this and your story is messy.
Maybe sexual sin isn't a theological subject to you.
Maybe it has your face.
Maybe it has your browser history.
Maybe it has somebody else's name attached to it.
Maybe it happened last night.
Maybe you've been sleeping beside someone you know you shouldn't be sleeping with.
Maybe pornography has followed you from adolescence into adulthood.
Maybe you're carrying memories nobody at church knows about.
Maybe you're living two lives.
Maybe people call you “brother.”
Maybe they call you “sister.”
Maybe they see the Bible verses you post.
They see you worship.
They see you smile.
But they don't see what happens when the door closes.
And maybe the hardest part of reading this isn't what Paul says about “the world.”
Maybe it's those terrifying little words:
“being called a brother...”
Because suddenly you're not looking outside anymore.
You're looking in a mirror.
And this is where I need you to hear something Christianity can never afford to lose:
Conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
The Gospel does not say your sin is harmless.
The Gospel says your sin was so serious that Christ went to a cross...
and His grace is so astonishing that the cross can still save you.
Jesus does not need you to pretend.
He already knows.
He knows what you watched.
He knows who you touched.
He knows what happened in that room.
He knows what you're craving.
He knows the affair.
He knows the addiction.
He knows the secret messages.
He knows the shame you keep burying underneath worship songs and Christian language.
And still...
the invitation of the Gospel is not:
“Hide better.”
It is:
Repent and come home.
The Greek New Testament uses μετάνοια — metanoia for repentance: a turning, a changed mind and direction before God.
Christian repentance isn't learning to become better at appearing holy.
It is bringing the real sinner into the light.
Because Jesus didn't die for your Christian image.
He died for you.
This is why we have to understand Paul correctly.
There are two disastrous ways to distort this passage.
One distortion says:
“Stay away from sinners.”
The other says:
“Sin doesn't matter.”
Paul allows neither.
The Christian does not retreat from lost people.
And the Christian does not normalize rebellion among those professing Christ.
We go toward the lost with the Gospel...
and we call the church toward holiness through the Gospel.
Truth without mission becomes isolation.
Mission without truth becomes compromise.
Jesus gives us something better:
truth full of grace, and grace that transforms.
Look at Christ Himself.
People accused Jesus of being a friend of tax collectors and sinners.
He ate where respectable religious people thought He shouldn't eat.
He spoke to people others avoided.
He touched people others considered unclean.
He allowed broken people near Him.
But nobody could honestly say Jesus celebrated their bondage.
When Jesus came near sinners, He did not become more like their sin.
Sinners encountered something in Him that called them out of it.
Think about the woman caught in adultery.
Jesus refused to join the bloodthirsty crowd seeking her destruction.
Yet His mercy never became moral indifference.
His grace carried a direction:
Go...
and leave your life of sin.
That is Jesus.
No stone in His hand.
No compromise on His lips.
Grace and truth.
Mercy and holiness.
Forgiveness and transformation.
Maybe that is what somebody in your life desperately needs.
Not your disgust.
Not your self-righteousness.
Not another Facebook post about how terrible “the world” has become.
Maybe they need you sitting across the table from them.
Listening.
Loving.
Refusing to lie about sin.
Refusing to treat them as though their sin has made them unreachable.
And eventually saying:
“Can I tell you what Jesus did for me?”
Because never forget this...
you were not born inside the Kingdom because you behaved better than everybody else.
You needed rescue too.
Every Christian testimony begins with someone who could not save himself.
Paul himself knew that.
The man writing these words had once persecuted the church.
He had breathed threats.
Christ met him anyway.
That does not minimize sexual sin.
It magnifies grace.
And grace isn't permission to stay chained.
Grace breaks chains.

Paul would later remind the Corinthians that sexually immoral people, idolaters, adulterers, thieves, greedy people, drunkards, revilers and swindlers would not inherit God's kingdom—and then he gave them three of the most beautiful words imaginable:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Not because they cleaned themselves sufficiently to impress God.
Paul continues with the language of washing, sanctification and justification in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
That is Christianity.
Not:
“Look how much better I am than those people.”
But:
“Look what Jesus did to someone like me.”
Maybe the sexually broken person you're avoiding is one Gospel conversation away from beginning a journey toward Christ.
Maybe the atheist you're afraid to befriend is watching to see whether Christians actually believe in grace.
Maybe the woman everyone whispers about is desperately wondering whether God could still want her.
Maybe the man whose reputation is ruined thinks church doors were built to keep people like him outside.
Maybe your prodigal child already knows what you condemn...
but has forgotten how deeply you love them.
Go toward them.
Not toward their sin.
Toward them.
Jesus did.
But if you are the one claiming Christ while secretly making peace with sin, don't use this article as an excuse.
Paul won't let you.
There is a massive difference between stumbling in a battle you desperately want Christ to win...
and settling into rebellion while demanding that nobody confront you.
A believer may fall.
A believer may struggle terribly.
A believer may need restoration, accountability, counseling, confession, prayer and brothers or sisters willing to walk beside them.
But Christianity never teaches us to rename darkness so we can comfortably remain inside it.
Jesus didn't shed His blood so we could decorate our chains.
He came to set captives free.
So maybe today isn't about somebody else.
Maybe this article found you.
No performance now.
No religious mask.
Just you and God.
What have you been hiding?
What relationship do you know needs to change?
What secret habit keeps pulling you back?
What compromise have you renamed because repentance would cost too much?
What would happen if instead of running from Jesus in shame...
you ran toward Him?
Peter failed spectacularly.
Jesus restored him.
The prodigal went into the far country.
The father received him home.
The thief reached the final hours of his life beside a cross...
and discovered that grace was still closer than he imagined.
Your scandal does not have to become the final sentence of your story.
Jesus Christ was crucified for sinners.
He was buried.
He rose again.
Forgiveness is real.
Grace is real.
Repentance is real.
Transformation is real.
And there is still room at the feet of Jesus for people whose lives have become things they never imagined they would become.
If this exposed something you've been hiding, don't perform for the comments.
But if you need to draw a line in the sand today, write:
If you need brothers and sisters to pray rather than condemn you, simply write:

And if Christ has already pulled you out of a place you thought would destroy you, tell somebody what He did. Your testimony might become the reason another ashamed person finally believes redemption is possible.
Not because every sentence is comfortable.
Send it privately to the person who thinks their scandal has placed them beyond grace.
And please don't stop at sharing articles.
Go love somebody.
Go listen.
Go tell somebody about Jesus.
Go be present without compromising truth.
Because Christians are not called to escape the mission field.
We are called to carry Christ into it.
Giving belongs to God before it belongs to any ministry.

If glorifying God is your desire, glorify Him first through faith in Christ, obedience, holiness, love, generosity, witness and a surrendered life. And if supporting this particular work is one expression of that generosity God places on your heart, we would be profoundly grateful to have you stand with us.
Stay close to Scripture.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite the person who walked away from church.
Invite seekers.
Invite lukewarm Christians who need awakening.
Even invite the unbeliever who doesn't know what to think about Jesus yet.
come to Jesus.
That matters infinitely more.
Because Gospel Warrior cannot save you.
A church membership cannot save you.
Religious behavior cannot save you.
Your reputation cannot save you.
Only Jesus Christ saves.
And maybe that is the deepest truth hiding inside Paul's uncomfortable words.
The world isn't our enemy to escape.
It is filled with people Christ died to save.
The church isn't a showroom for people who never struggled.
It is supposed to be a people transformed by the crucified and risen King.
So stop throwing stones at people Jesus told us to reach.
Stop calling compromise “grace.”
Stop calling isolation “holiness.”
Stop protecting secret sin with Christian language.
Come into the light.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where forgiveness is needed.
Restore the repentant.
Confront what destroys.
Love the lost.
Guard the church.
Preach Christ.
And remember:
Somebody else's scandal may be the chapter where Jesus is about to begin writing grace.
And the page you thought shame had ruined forever may still be wet with the ink of redemption.
